summary.overview: This chapter compares the three dominant data models — relational, document, and graph — and the query languages that go with them. Its real point is that the model you pick shapes how you think about your problem and how complex your application code becomes, so you should match the model to your data's shape and access patterns rather than treating any one model as universally best.

sections.heading: Relational Model Versus Document Model
takeaways: Object-relational mismatch: applications model data as objects while relational databases store tables, so a translation layer (e.g. an ORM) is needed — and it can never fully hide the difference.

NoSQL/document databases rose in the 2010s driven by: desire for greater and easier scalability, preference for open-source software, specialized query operations, and frustration with restrictive relational schemas.

The document model naturally fits one-to-many hierarchies (nested JSON), but handles many-to-one and many-to-many poorly because join support is weak or absent; the relational answer is normalization — don't duplicate human-meaningful data like city names, since every copy must be updated when it changes.

Schema-on-read (document): the schema is implicit and interpreted when data is read, so old and new formats are handled in application code. Schema-on-write (relational): the schema is explicit and enforced, so format changes require migrations such as ALTER TABLE.

Documents win on data locality when an application loads a whole tree of related data at once, but updates usually force a rewrite of the entire document; the two models are converging (relational systems added JSON/XML support, document systems like RethinkDB added joins).

sections.heading: Query Languages for Data
takeaways: Declarative languages (SQL) say what data you want and how to transform it, not how to fetch it — they are more concise, let the database optimize execution (query planner) without changing queries, and lend themselves to parallel execution; imperative code spells out each operation step by step.

Declarative is not just SQL: CSS is declarative (a selector plus desired styling) versus verbose imperative DOM JavaScript that is longer, harder to follow, and doesn't automatically revert when state changes.

MapReduce sits between declarative and imperative: you write map and reduce functions (low-level distributed programming); the functions must be pure and cannot run extra database queries, they are harder to write correctly than a single query, and they give the query optimizer less room to help.

sections.heading: Graph-Like Data Models
takeaways: Property graph model: each vertex has a unique id, sets of incoming/outgoing edges, and key-value properties; each edge has an id, a tail vertex, a head vertex, a label, and properties. Any vertex can connect to any other, and different labels let one graph hold many kinds of relationships — natural for highly interconnected many-to-many data.

Cypher is a declarative query language for property graphs (pattern syntax like (person)-[:BORN_IN]->(city)); Gremlin is the imperative counterpart; SQL can express graph queries via recursive CTEs (WITH RECURSIVE), but awkwardly.

Triple-stores record facts as subject-predicate-object triples queried with SPARQL; Datalog is their foundation — a declarative language whose rules can be reused and combined (good for complex data, less convenient for simple one-off queries) — and graphs make schemas easy to evolve.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Applications are built by layering one data model on top of another, each layer hiding the complexity beneath; the model you choose profoundly shapes how you think about the problem.
No single model wins: relational and document models are converging because they complement each other, so pick the model (and query language) that fits your data's shape and access patterns.
